And so, yeah, those columns are weekly musings, so to speak. But yeah, to answer your question, consumer AI. I think the funny thing about consumer, especially when you ask a lot of other investors, is that it's been a bit of a bad word recently. A lot of people have been spooked. A lot of people have missed a lot of bets. Even some of the bets that they've taken haven't necessarily panned out. And I would argue that the reason for that has a lot to do with just human nature. I think human beings are largely fixed. Like, I don't think we've evolved much in the last two years. I don't think we've evolved much in the last 50. I think what ends up happening is that the tools that we have available to us do change. And I think for a very long time, the tools that we had were kind of good enough. Like, if I needed to go from point A to point B, Uber was more than good. If I needed groceries delivered, DoorDash, Instacart was much more than satisfactory. I think what we're seeing now is something that extends beyond just incremental. And I think AI is kind of the catalyst for that, where you start to see 100,000x improvements over existing consumer experiences. And so I would argue that we're on the cusp of a consumer renaissance. And I'm particularly excited about the new crop of companies that are being forged today. That will be extremely meaningful in the years to come.

[SPEAKER_01]
Wow. I want to just double click on the consumer renaissance. What does that fully look like? Is there like an example? Consumer renaissance is a strong, that's a strong word. And today, there's like a lot of mantras. Totally. From all the columns that you've been doing that I want to jump into. But this mantra, I haven't heard about it. So tell me more about that.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I think in a lot of ways, the landscape is being reimagined. And there's an abundance. I'm a former consultant. So I think in frameworks, there's an abundance in frameworks that you can kind of apply to the category. I think one fun one to dig into is democratization, right? So if you think about the different eras of technology, I think technologies existed as a tool that democratized access, for example, to a lot of different things that were either prohibitively expensive, or not within the realm of possibility for most people. Case in point, therapy, right? When you think about the first era of tech solving therapeutic needs, it largely looked like a phone book just put online, right? Where you had marketplaces that sought to broker a connection between a patient and a therapist. Over time, you started to see technologies kind of solve to some extent that therapeutic conditioning, where they were able to either support a therapist in running their business, or, you know, being some type of emotional groundedness in the form of, you know, headspace or something to that effect, to support people through their medical journeys. I think if I think about what AI stands to represent today, you can start to play around with AI therapists, right? Where you can have a therapeutic offering wrapped in an AI like experience. And what that solves for is being able to potentially democratize that access to a broader cohort of people who can't necessarily afford, you know, the $400 a visit that therapy usually involves, or may not have schedules that align. So you can start to think of, all right, I'm going through a crisis of some sort, I need support, it's 3am. How do I kind of solve for that? And technology can show up in very different ways than has been the

[SPEAKER_01]
case previously. Wow. Actually, you're skipping ahead on some of my notes here. I want to talk about AI and health. You actually, in one of your other columns, you wrote about AI should make us more human, not less human. So I want to understand how we can leverage AI to have a deeper human experience. And then even maybe another quote that I read in one of your columns was that, folks, this might be a countercultural moment, where we shift from optimize me, which is like AI is very optimized focus, to liberate me. And this was like referring to some folks who might be starting meds today, which is becoming like very ubiquitous, but they will want to get off of meds or whatever type of health things in the future. And like, there's no real off ramp right now. And so there is like a future that looks like, I want AI to liberate me versus like, optimize me.

[SPEAKER_00]
Totally. I think AI to date has found a lot of success in productivity, which is meaningful, and especially in work context. You have a lot of talk about 10x, 100x engineers, which obviously is impressive and powerful and is changing almost the physics of various businesses. As a consumer investor, and as a, you know, an aspiring anthropologist, I'm interested in kind of the cultural underpinnings of technology and what it can solve for. And I like to think of behaviors, I like to think of patterns, I like to think of being able to solve for the human experience. I think one of the realms or dimensions that I get particularly excited about is indeed healthcare, because I think healthcare to date has been some version of emergency triage. Something goes horrendously wrong, and you point to the healthcare system to try to course correct. Sometimes it's too late. Sometimes it requires a ton of resources. And I think it strips patients and people to some extent of their agency. I like the idea of using technology for folks to reclaim a bit of that agency and self-empower, where you move from something that feels entirely reactive to something that feels way more proactive. And there's like a guiding hand along the way to support you in your healthcare journey. And so when I think about solutions like Council Health, which falls within the GV portfolio, when I think about Aura, which was a company that I was involved in back when I was living a previous life of Forerunner Ventures, I love the idea of being able to put technology into the hands of individuals and giving them the tools to be better equipped to solve for the healthcare journey.

[SPEAKER_01]
Wow. I want to, since you brought up Aura, I do want to go into that place too. AI and hardware, if you will, right now. Yeah. So you worked with Aura when you were at Forerunner. I'm curious, and obviously like Aura, many people, I have my whoop on right now, so apologies. But I know a lot of people who wear Aura, they recently just had some big announcements on revenue marks and just like dominated a market. And I think they just came out with like a new version of the ring. I'm curious if you can share any details around just like that experience working with their team, that product, and then consumer hardware in general.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, totally. So consumer hardware, I think inspires the same level of caution that just consumer in general, where if you talk to investors, everyone proclaims that hardware is hard. And I think that's largely true, right? Like I think the facts do remain that oftentimes margins aren't as attractive as software. Iterative cycles look very different. You have to manage manufacturing complexities. There's a long list of things that make hardware categorically difficult. That said, when it works, it can explode. And I think hardware is probably one of the places that's most likely to inspire joy and delight, especially if done well. And doing well oftentimes look like becoming an invisible, natural extension of the human experience. I think one of the things, and I can speak to Aura specifically, I think one of the things that team was largely successful at was almost reconciling two inherent tensions. On one hand, they made a device that felt so seamless, so non-obstructive, so natural. It's a ring on your finger. It looks like every other piece of jewelry. It's tasteful. And it was able to grant you superpowers in understanding your health. But at the same time, they were able to balance that against it being kind of low-key, like a quiet luxury, right? Like there was a lot of signaling associated with the ring. In its early days, they did a really good job of collaborating with celebrities. And so when you walked, when you saw the Oscars or the Grammys, and you noticed that Will Smith was wearing an aura ring, you kind of questioned to yourself, it's like, what's going on over there? And they were able to manage that tension very, very well. And as extension of that, I think they were able to, in a way that I haven't seen across a lot of other consumer brands born from the Bay or born from the coast, they managed to really quickly cross the chasm, which is to say that they created a product that was appealing not just for tech bros and nerds hanging out in San Francisco. You had folks like my mom who purchased a ring. Anecdotally, it was wild to come home from New York at the time I was living in the Bay. And so when I visited home, I was shocked to hear that my mom was asking about an aura ring. She had no idea that I was involved in any capacity. It was just something that fell onto her radar and she was thinking about a purchase decision. And I thought that was exciting because it felt almost like the company that you saw act as a toddler kind of grow up into its mature years. And come into your house. Yeah, right. It was almost the equivalent of having like a illustration on the fridge, where it was like a stamp of approval that said that, oh, this could be a meaningfully large company because it was able to tackle a demographic that wasn't immediately obvious. As it turns out, everyone sleeps. And so the TAM is immediately obvious. But it was really interesting to see it float out of some of the more normal places into places that I didn't expect.

[SPEAKER_01]
Wow. Yeah, I agree with the virtue signaling. Like, I really start to understand other people if they're wearing a whoop. Like, I've started so many conversations or anytime I'm like talking to a founder or someone else from like a networking standpoint, I'll always ask them like, how do you like your whoop? How do you like the aura ring? Or to be honest, is vice versa as well. So I can be in a conversation with somebody and they'll just stop and say like, how do you like the whoop? What's the difference between a whoop and aura? All these different things. So I think some of the like hardware per se is now becoming similar to like wearing a certain type of watch, a certain type of blouse, certain type of fashion item. It's actually becoming like a story that you tell. Yeah. Which I think is genius for aura to like click in there because this is clearly not necessarily a fashion statement. It's a performance statement. I mean, yeah, it's an opinion of sorts. But aura ring was probably one of the first and still maybe one of the like handful of only things that could actually be like an interesting fashion statement, but still be like a clear like health.
